source.text:
> Damn that sounds amazing

Well, I like it :-). I don't have any sharable photos handy and the architectural CAD, sight lines, acoustic reflection map, environmental specs, etc were all delivered in a client binder but every page has our address on it. You can get an accurate idea of what it's like with an image search for "High-end custom-built home theater" or "Hollywood studio screening room." It looks like the top 10% of those. IMHO, the nearest theater that has a better image and equal sound is the 15-perf full IMAX over an hour's drive away (one of only ~30 15-perf IMAX theaters in the US (not strip mall LieMAX :-)).

But I led with "Well, I like it" because as an engineer, I know there's technically 'correct' visual and audio reproduction to a given spec (eg BT.2020 color space. 1000 nit peak dynamic range and 10,000:1 contrast ratio), but there's no such thing as a perfect theater or screening room. IMHO, the goal should be the closest to technically correct reproduction possible within a given space, budget and set of preferences. The skill (and fun) is in getting the best solve within the constraints.

> you really put the research into this

Actually, I didn't do much. I'm the second owner and the custom room (as well as the house around it) was built by the original owner. He actually spent way more money than anyone should have but he didn't know anything about A/V or tech in general. Fortunately, he selected a very high-end custom theater design vendor who knew what they were doing (I've been in a room they did at Dreamworks and they did one for Spielberg).

Shortly after the house was completed apparently the owner got addicted to meth and, over a period of three years, pretty much destroyed the life he'd built. Sad story. By the time I saw it the house was a distressed asset and we heard all this from a realtor working for the bank. The gorgeous home had become an open drug house in the middle of a neighborhood of high-end custom homes. Apparently there were 300 police calls in one year and the place was thrashed, including smashed windows and custom doors from police raid battering rams, fire damage from flash bang grenades and even year-hold Taco Bell burritos thrown in a $35K Swarovski chandelier. There was trash (including syringes) over every inch of the floor and we bought it as-is without ever seeing the basement because the stairwell down was so full of trash, it took a crew in Hazmat suits days to clear it. We called 1-800-JUNK, they opened the front door, took one look, said "Nope" turned-around and walked out :-).

But the lender's appraisal just a few years earlier had valued the place at millions before it was nuked - and when I looked in the non-functioning theater, which required crawling in with a flashlight, I saw the designer's nameplate and knew that just that room alone, without electronics, was worth more than the bank's asking price. So we had a friend who's a custom home builder go through the entire house and develop a detailed punch list. He said it was the worst looking house he'd ever seen but assured us it was all surface damage - and the bones underneath weren't just good, they were great. It took over six months and a few hundred thousand to strip it down to drywall everywhere (and studs in many areas). The contractors did new flooring, finishes and fixtures throughout and I restored the theater back to working myself while doing an upgrade to 4K and expanding the 7.2 audio to 7.2.4. A year after we bought it, the house was appraised at well over double what we paid including the full rebuild.

After closing, the realtor told us we were the first buyers to actually even finish walking through it, much less make an offer :-). So, yeah... it was a 'fixer' so bad the bank took our low-ball. With the theater I happened to know exactly what I was looking at and that I could restore and upgrade it all myself (plus reverse engineer the oddball home automation system that was built into every wall and no longer working).
